content.title: Limited experiments, limited justifications, requires additional knowledge
content.review:
[The acknowledgment section might be violating the blind review.]

This paper claims to simplify and improve recently proposed automatic curriculum learning methods. Their experiments in section 4 are very limited to a single setup and most of the simplifications are not well-justified by any new results. Their proposed algorithm in section 5 assumes the presence of addition ordering information about tasks which needs a more thorough comparison to other related works.

Section 4 introduces some simplifications. They “recommend” a few choices by referencing the figures in [2], essentially reiterating the contributions of [2] and presenting no new results. Then they propose modifications to \eps-greedy with window algorithm of [1] by presenting results on one task. They propose to remove the moving average and essentially reintroducing the naive algorithm of [2].

Section 5 proposes a new algorithm that relies on a additional knowledge of ordering of tasks. It based on a measure called “mastering rate” for a task that it is converted to an “attention” value by incorporating the ordering information. Attention values are propagated in one extra step.

Positives:
MR algorithm might be good but no compelling experiments are presented.

Negatives:
- The experiments are limited to one set of tasks introduced by this work. It is not clear if it is a good benchmark for automated curriculum learning. Section 4 does not compare to any method that does not perform any automated curriculum learning.
- Fig. 6 and 7, the main figures of this paper, show that the baseline gets almost zero reward in most of the experiments. Basically, they are beating a weak baseline without explaining why it has failed. Maybe other algorithms in the previous work would work better in this setting.
- There is a mistake in analyzing the algorithm of [1]. [1] does not exactly fit in Teacher-Student framework because they use Exp3.S policy that combines Boltzmann exploration with an \eps-greedy strategy. They also have a hyperparameter \eta that acts as the temperature of the softmax.
- There is no ablation study on the importance and effect of each of the last 2 steps of the MR algorithm (Eq. 1, 2, 3). Does one need the ordering?
- Works such as [3] are also related because of the use of additional ordering information.


[1] Graves et al
[2] Matiisen et al
[3] Pentina, Anastasia, Viktoriia Sharmanska, and Christoph H. Lampert. "Curriculum learning of multiple tasks." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2015.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We are grateful for the time taken to elaborate this detailed review provided by Reviewer 1, for their careful reading of the paper, and their suggestions. In our response we ask for some additional insights on some points to help us improve the paper.

1. "They propose modifications to \eps-greedy with window algorithm of [1]": to our knowledge, there is no "window algorithm" in [1]. We may have misread this paper of maybe Reviewer 1 refers to [2]?

2. "They propose to remove the moving average and essentially reintroducing the naive algorithm of [2].": This is not true. The naive algorithm of [2] uses a moving average too (with \alpha=0.2 recommended). We are not reintroducing an algorithm presented in [2].

3. "Section 4 does not compare to any method that does not perform any automated curriculum learning.": We don't understand what Reviewer 1 means here or what he would expect.

4. "There is a mistake in analyzing the algorithm of [1]. [...] the temperature of the softmax.": We don't understand what Reviewer 1 comments in our paper. We don't analyze algorithm 1 and we don't want it to fit into Teacher-Student framework.

content.title: violation of anonymity, poor writing
content.review: The paper contains an acknowledge section with people's names, which is a clear violation of anonymity. In addition, the submission obviously rushed and incomplete. The writing is very poor. There are only 7 references. The experimental results are limited to toy tasks, and the result section has only 8 lines. I don't think this paper worth a serious consideration at the current state.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
Thank you for the time you took to review the paper! 

The presence of the acknowledgment section with people's names is completely stupid... Is it eliminatory?

We completely understand that you don't want to spend too much time on a paper that is not worth attention. However, your review is not currently very useful for us. So, regarding your review, we would be glad to have your view on the following questions:

- You qualify the writing as "poor". Is it poor because "There are only 7 references. The experimental results are limited to toy tasks, and the result section has only 8 lines.", or is it poor for other reasons? In the last case, could you give us some clues on how to improve it?

- You don't appreciate the few number of references. We cited only the very relevant papers and  prefered (probably wrongly) to correctly present (in few pages) the theory. Is it eliminatory? Is it a so bad idea?

- You don't appreciate the use of only toys environment. We chose such environments for several reasons:

1. As far as we know, Gym-MiniGrid is the only library allowing to easily design tasks and hence create curriculums.
2. In order to evaluate the quality of a curriculum algorithm, no need to have tasks that look complex (such as the game of Go, etc...), but only to have tasks that are very hard (or impossible to learn) alone (e.g. toy tasks with a small max_step threshold).
3. Not taking toy tasks makes the whole process very slow for no reason. This doesn't help to evaluate the quality of the curriculum algorithm.
4. With just toy tasks, we can show our algorithm performs better.

Do you think these arguments are admissible? If yes, should we make them appear in the paper?

- You don't appreciate the very short result section. What is missing inside? We showed how our algorithm outperformed the other algorithm on two different curriculums.

content.title: Reject due to lack of sufficient evaluation
content.review:
Pros:
1) Some of the simplifications might be useful.
2) The MR algorithm sounds interesting.
Cons: 
1) The acknowledgement section was left in the review draft, violating anonymous review.
2) Results do not seem particularly compelling (presented on just one task, and unclear how it generalizes to other tasks).
3) Some of the justifications seem a bit strange. For eg, quoting from the paper: "Why this assumption? Because it can't be otherwise"
content.confidence: 1: The reviewer's evaluation is an educated guess
